text:
After successful pollination, kernels pass through a grain-filling sequence sometimes described as the milk stage, dough stage, and dent stage (when a visible dent forms at the crown of each kernel as starch accumulates and moisture drops). A "milk line" is visible on a cut kernel and progressively moves down toward the base of the kernel as the grain matures.

Physiological maturity is reached when a dark abscission layer (the "black layer") forms at the kernel's attachment point to the cob, at which point dry-matter accumulation stops; at this point kernel moisture is typically still fairly high (on the order of 30% or more), so the grain is not yet dry enough for safe storage and normally needs further field drying or mechanical drying before harvest and storage (see the harvest and drying topics). Husks turning brown and papery is a useful field indicator that the crop is approaching maturity, but the black-layer check is the more reliable physiological indicator.
